title: Memecoins & Bonding Curves
objectives: Understand how a bonding curve prices a token purely as a function of its supply
Trace a memecoin launch from bonding curve to graduated liquidity pool
Compute the early-buyer edge and why late buyers are the exit liquidity
Spot the structural traps: rug pulls, honeypots, and snipers

steps.title: The Bonding Curve: Price From Supply Alone
steps.body:
A <Term id="bonding_curve">bonding curve</Term> is a mathematical rule that sets a token's price based only on how many tokens have been sold. There is no order book, no market maker, no counterparty. The contract *is* the market.

A common shape is a simple upward curve: `price = k * supply`. The very first token might cost a fraction of a cent; the ten-thousandth costs ten times more.

The mechanics:

- **Buy** → supply increases → price rises along the curve → the next buyer pays more.
- **Sell** → supply decreases → price falls back down the curve → the seller gets back less per token than the curve's top.

The curve guarantees **liquidity** - you can always buy or sell against it - but it does not guarantee **value**. It is a pricing machine, not a store of worth. This is exactly why memecoins launch here: anyone can spin up a token with instant, automatic liquidity and a built-in rising price chart that feels like momentum even when nothing real is happening.

The essential asymmetry is baked into the math. The earliest buyers ride the cheap part of the curve, and every subsequent buyer pushes the price up *for them*. When the last buyer stops coming, the curve runs in reverse - and there is no one left to sell to except the curve itself, which pays out along the way down.
hints: Price is a function of supply. Buying raises supply and price; selling lowers both.
The curve always provides liquidity - but liquidity is not the same as value.

steps.title: Launch to Graduation: The Memecoin Lifecycle
steps.body:
Most fair-launch memecoins follow the same arc:

1. **Deploy** - a creator launches a token on a bonding curve (think Pump.fun-style). No presale, no VC. The curve is the only seller.
2. **Snipe** - the fastest bots buy in the first blocks, grabbing the cheapest part of the curve before humans can even read the ticker.
3. **Climb** - as buyers pile in, the price rises along the curve and the chart prints green. Early buyers are already up multiples.
4. **Graduate** - once enough capital is committed, the token 'graduates': the accumulated funds are used to seed a real <Term id="liquidity_pool">liquidity pool</Term> (often on a DEX), and the token trades freely.
5. **The dump** - early buyers and snipers sell into the fresh liquidity. If no new wave of buyers replaces them, the price bleeds back to dust.

Here is the structural truth: a bonding curve has no positive-sum outcome for the crowd. Every dollar of profit for an early seller must come from a later buyer's deposit. Total buy-ins minus total sell-outs equals the loss. It is a rearrangement of money, not a creation of it.

The snipers are not 'lucky'. They run infrastructure that buys in milliseconds, precisely timed to be first on the curve. The retail buyer arriving on a viral tweet is *structurally* the exit liquidity - not because they are stupid, but because they are late in a zero-sum queue. Understanding this does not make you immune. It makes the losses legible instead of mysterious.
hints: Graduation just converts curve liquidity into pool liquidity - it does not create value.
In a bonding curve, one trader's gain is literally another's deposit. The crowd nets negative.

steps.title: Under the Hood: Rugs, Honeypots, and Sniper Defense
steps.body:
The curve is honest math. The *creator* is not necessarily honest, and most memecoin losses come from traps layered on top.

**The lethal patterns:**

- **Rug pull** - the creator holds a large bag (or the LP tokens) and dumps, or pulls the liquidity entirely. Price goes to zero in one transaction.
- **<Term id="honeypot">Honeypot</Term>** - you can buy but the contract blocks selling, or applies a hidden 99% sell tax. Your money is trapped by design; the only exit is for the creator.
- **Mint authority** - if the creator can mint unlimited new supply, your share is silently diluted to nothing.
- **Freeze / blacklist** - the contract can freeze wallets, so the team can lock everyone out and drain.

**Defenses that reduce (not remove) risk:**

- Check for a **revoked mint authority** and **renounced or burned LP**.
- Inspect the contract for sell-blocks, transfer taxes, and freeze functions before buying.
- Prefer tokens where liquidity is **burned or locked** in a time vault.
- Treat social virality as a warning, not a signal - hype is the mechanism that delivers your money to the early wallets.

The deepest lesson is about asymmetry. A rug or honeypot can take 100% of your position while your theoretical upside is capped by how many new buyers arrive after you. When the downside is total and the upside depends on strangers showing up later, you are not investing - you are playing a game with negative expectations dressed in a rocket emoji. Being able to say 'I understand this and I still choose not to play' is a skill.
hints: Rugs and honeypots make your downside 100% while your upside still depends on later buyers.
Always check: revoke mint authority, burn/lock LP, no sell-block or freeze functions.

questions.prompt: On a bonding curve where price rises with supply, what happens when you sell?
options: Price stays the same because you are the seller
Supply decreases, price falls back along the curve, and you receive less per token than the current top
questions.explainRight: Selling reduces supply, so the price walks back down the curve. The curve pays you the area below your sell point, which is less per token than the peak. The curve is symmetric: rising buys, falling sells.
questions.explainWrong: A bonding curve prices by supply. Selling reduces supply and moves price down the same curve you climbed, so your payout per token is below the top. It is directionally symmetric to buying.

questions.prompt: Why is a bonding-curve memecoin structurally zero-sum for the crowd of traders?
options: Because the price always goes down
Because the curve creates no value - every seller's profit is funded by a later buyer's deposit, so the group as a whole can only lose to fees and the creator
Because only one person can ever sell
questions.explainRight: The curve only rearranges money between participants. Total buy-ins minus total sell-outs equals the net loss to the crowd. Early sellers win precisely because later buyers fund them. No production, no cash flows, no value creation.
questions.explainWrong: The curve is a redistribution engine. Profits for early sellers come dollar-for-dollar from later buyers, so the crowd nets negative once fees and creator bags are accounted for. It is not that price only falls - it is that the system creates nothing.

options: A token that pays passive income
A token you can buy but cannot sell - the contract blocks selling or applies a near-total sell tax, trapping your money by design
A token with very high liquidity
A token that is audited and safe
questions.explainRight: A honeypot lets you buy and then blocks the exit - sell restrictions, hidden sell taxes, or freeze functions. The creator is the only one who can get out. It looks tradable right up until you try to sell.
questions.explainWrong: A honeypot traps buyers: purchases succeed, sales fail or are taxed to near-zero. The contract is built so only the creator can exit. Always check for sell-blocks, transfer taxes, and freeze functions before buying.

questions.prompt: Which set of checks most reduces - though never eliminates - memecoin rug risk?
options: Checking the token's emoji and community size
Verify revoked mint authority, burned/locked LP, and absence of sell-block or freeze functions in the contract
Buying only tokens trending on social media
Waiting one day after launch to buy
questions.explainRight: Revoked mint authority stops dilution, burned/locked LP stops a liquidity pull, and no sell-block or freeze means the team cannot trap you. These checks reduce known rug vectors, but smart-contract risk and zero-sum dynamics remain - so risk is lowered, never removed.
questions.explainWrong: The durable checks are technical: no mint authority, LP burned or locked, and no sell-block or freeze logic. Hype, community size, and waiting all feel safer but do not address the actual mechanisms of a rug. Even with all checks, memecoins remain highly risky.
